items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
items.content:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.

The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."

Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.

Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."

Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.

Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.

Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.

Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

items.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
items.summary: browsers
items.content:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-82445 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Description The SQL status backend serialises per-URL metadata into a single column by concatenating a tabulation
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-82445 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Description The SQL status backend serialises per-URL metadata into a single column by concatenating a tabulation, the key, an equals sign and the value, with no escaping. On read-back the string is split on the same two characters, so the round trip is not injective: a value that contains a tabulation returns as one or more additional keys that were never written. Values on that path are supplied by crawled servers. `FetcherBolt` records the raw `Location` header of a redirect as `_redirTo`, and `_redirTo` is part of the default `metadata.persist` set, so a redirect whose `Location` contains a tabulation followed by `key=value` pairs introduces those keys into the crawler's own control metadata on the next scheduling cycle. Several control keys are read without a prefix, so the injected keys are live: `http.proxy.host`, `http.proxy.port`, `http.proxy.user` and `http.proxy.pass` among them, as well as scheduling and request-shaping keys such as `depth`, `max.depth`, `crawl.delay`, `http.content.limit` and `isSitemap`. Where a proxy manager is configured, the consequence is not limited to corrupted scheduling data. `SingleProxyManager.getProxy(Metadata)` consults the per-URL metadata first and returns what it finds, so an injected proxy host and port take precedence over the operator's configured proxy and subsequent fetches, together with any configured `Authorization` header, are routed through a host the crawled content chose. A related defect in `AbstractStatusUpdaterBolt` compounds this: an injected `status.store.as.is.with.nextfetchdate` that is not a valid instant escapes the enclosing try/catch and stops the bolt, and because the stored row is replayed the failure repeats. Deployments using the OpenSearch or Solr status backends are unaffected, because those serialise metadata structurally. Mitigation Upgrade to 4.0.0, where the metadata column is written in an escaped form behind a format marker, rows written by earlier versions are still decoded unchanged, and the stored next-fetch-date is parsed defensively. The fix does not repair rows written before the upgrade. Operators using the SQL status backend should inspect the metadata column of an existing status table for tabulation characters and remove the affected rows, and should assume any proxy credentials configured for the crawl may have been exercised through an attacker-chosen proxy and rotate them. Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove `_redirTo` from `metadata.persist` to close the demonstrated path, though other crawled values reaching persisted metadata remain. Credit Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept. Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated and reported by Apache StormCrawler. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-24T10:39:17.246Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-82445

items.title: 2035 came early
items.summary: nix, wasm
items.content:
tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox .

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript.

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev .

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev .

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability.

I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix .

It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster.  especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: GrapheneOS shows off how it plans RCS support without Google Messages
items.content:
RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app shows how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

As virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS users, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

We made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ

There’s still no firm timeline for this new RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-82444 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Description `CookieConverter.getCookies` decides which stored cookies to attach to an outbound request. The applicability check is nested inside a test for the presence of a `Domain` attribute, so a cookie without one, which is the ordinary form of a session cookie, skips scoping entirely and is returned for whatever target URL was passed. RFC 6265 requires the opposite: a cookie with no `Domain` attribute is host-only and belongs to the host that set it. Two further defects sit in the same method. The domain comparison has no notion of a registrable domain, so a `Domain` value of `com` matches every host under it, and the comparison returns true when it throws, so a failure to evaluate the check admits the cookie. Neither the converter nor `MetadataTransfer`, which carries the stored cookie to outlinks, ever considers the host that issued it. Cookie handling is opt-in: it requires `http.use.cookies` to be set to true, which is not the default, and the cookie key to be listed in `metadata.transfer`. The documented recipe does not work as written, because the `metadata.transfer` example in the internals documentation names `set-cookie` while the key present in metadata is `protocol.set-cookie` and the transfer matches key names exactly. Deployments affected are therefore those where an operator determined the correct key, enabled cookie handling and crawls an authenticated site whose pages link or redirect to other hosts. In that case the session cookie of the authenticated origin is sent to those hosts. Mitigation Upgrade to 4.0.0, where a cookie without a `Domain` attribute is sent only to the host that set it, a single-label domain is rejected and the domain check fails closed. Because the protocol does not yet record the host that issued a cookie, cookies without a `Domain` attribute are not sent at all until that host is recorded; operators relying on cookie transfer will notice this. The documentation error is corrected in the same release. Users who cannot upgrade immediately should confine an authenticated crawl to a topology whose URL filters keep it on the origin that issued the credentials, and should not rely on cookie scoping as a boundary. Rotating session credentials used for such crawls is advisable. Credit Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept. items.title: Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
items.summary: mobile, privacy
items.content:
Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. 1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. 2

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. 2

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS. 3

items.title: Protests in Chicago After Google Warns Schools About Disabling AI Feature
items.content:
This story first appeared at The 74 , a nonprofit news site covering education. Sign up for free newsletters from The 74 to get more like this in your inbox.

Pushback on the use of artificial intelligence in the classroom is seeing renewed fervor after tensions flared this month between some U.S. school districts and one of the biggest tech giants in the world.

Protests popped up Wednesday in Cambridge, Massachusetts and in Chicago, where the city’s school district recently blocked student access to generative AI , which includes ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini. The backlash comes at a critical flashpoint for the future of AI in education. Google sparked an uproar earlier this month when it said that schools that ban AI won’t be able to use search because AI is so embedded in the technology.

Chicago Public Schools has yet to plan its response to Google’s announcement, but a CPS spokesperson said in a statement that the district was “actively exploring all options to independently suppress” the AI overview that appears at the top of Google searches. If CPS cannot provide students access to the search engine without its AI feature, the district will “look to other search solutions,” the spokesperson said.

The question of whether, and how, CPS could turn off Google’s AI features points to a dilemma at the core of Wednesday’s protests: determining the extent to which tech companies should be involved in public education .

About 30 people huddled together outside Google’s office in Chicago’s West Loop, shouting chants such as “Hey Google, nice try. We don’t want your Gemini.” Most of the protesters were parents and educators, but the demonstration included some students who voiced their own skepticism about whether AI is beneficial for themselves and their peers.

“We are owed lessons and feedback from the people CPS hired, people who are passionate and dedicated to making learning fun,” Reese Mackey, a 16-year-old Kenwood Academy High School junior said at the protest. “Not by a bot whose only job is to be a yes man and compile random sources from the internet for a nonsensical answer.”

If AI is so embedded into Google’s search engine, then it might be time for schools to step back and reassess whether to use Google at all, said Cassie Creswell, executive director of Illinois Families for Public Schools, which led the rally in Chicago.

“That really shouldn’t be our gateway to human knowledge, and so we need to draw a line there,” Creswell said.

In a statement to Chalkbeat, a Google spokesperson wrote that the company was taking steps to improve its search functions for classrooms, such as through piloting its “Guided Learning” feature that uses AI to walk students through a problem step-by-step rather than providing quick answers.

The conflict with Google is just the latest in a growing movement of parents, educators, and school administrators concerned about how students’ AI usage — as well as screen time generally — may negatively impact learning. Those worries have ramped up under the Trump administration, which has largely been friendly with the AI industry. The proliferation of the ever-evolving technology, in turn, has left schools scrambling to place guardrails on its usage.

“We really need real policy…not just a guidebook with suggestions that dump the burden on teachers and kids,” Creswell told reporters.

Some cities are putting stringent AI policies in place, most notably New York City under Mayor Zohran Mamdani . Just before this school year started, the city banned the use of student-facing AI, which includes chatbots, from preschool through eighth grade . Then, at the end of October, Chalkbeat obtained a list of nearly 40 products flagged by the city’s Education Department for their AI usage, such as Grammarly and Kahoot.

items.title: The state of SIMD in Rust in 2026
items.content:
A lot of progress was made since last year, and I made some of it!

After last year's survey I started contributing to the SIMD library that seemed the most promising. One thing led to another, and now I'm a maintainer of Fearless SIMD. To avoid a conflict of interest, I invited authors of other libraries ( std::simd , wide , pulp , macerator ) to review and provide feedback on a draft of this article. However, I retained editorial control, and all mistakes are my own. This year's survey is more in-depth than my previous one. So buckle up, and let's take it... from the top! What’s SIMD? Why SIMD?

Hardware that does arithmetic is cheap, so any CPU made this century has plenty of it. But you still only have one instruction decoding block and it is hard to get it to go fast, so the arithmetic hardware is vastly underutilized. To get around the instruction decoding bottleneck, you can feed the CPU a batch of numbers all at once for a single arithmetic operation like addition. Hence the name: “single instruction, multiple data,” or SIMD. Instead of adding two numbers together, you can add two batches or “vectors” of numbers and it takes about the same amount of time as doing just one addition. On recent x86 chips these batches can be up to 512 bits in size, so in theory you can get an 8x speedup for math on f64 or a 64x speedup on u8 . In practice it can run both slower and faster . Instruction sets

Historically, SIMD instructions were added after the CPU architecture was already designed, so SIMD is an extension with its own marketing name on each architecture. ARM calls theirs “NEON”, and all 64-bit ARM CPUs have it. WebAssembly doesn’t have a marketing department, so they just call theirs “WebAssembly 128-bit packed SIMD extension”. 64-bit x86 shipped with one called “SSE2” which has basic instructions for 128-bit vectors, but later they added a whole menagerie of extensions on top of that, with SSE 4.2 adding more operations, AVX and AVX2 adding 256-bit vectors and AVX-512 adding 512-bit vectors and even more operations. The word “later” in the above paragraph creates a problem. Does this CPU have that instruction?

If you’re running a program on an x86_64 CPU, it’s not a given that the CPU has any particular SIMD extension. So by default the compiler isn’t allowed to use instructions beyond SSE2 because that won’t work on all x86_64 CPUs. There are two ways around this problem. If you work for a company that only ever runs their binaries on their own servers or on a public cloud, you can just assert that they’re all recent enough to at least have AVX2 that was introduced over 10 years ago, and have the program crash or misbehave if it ever runs on anything without AVX2: RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3' cargo build --release However, if you are distributing the binaries for other people to run, that’s not really an option. Instead you can do something called function multiversioning: compile the same function multiple times for different SIMD extensions, and when the program actually runs, check what features the CPU supports and select the appropriate version based on that. Fortunately, this problem only exists on x86. ARM made NEON mandatory on its 64-bit CPUs and hasn't really added useful SIMD extensions after that (more on that later). WebAssembly makes you compile two different binaries, one with SIMD and one without, and use JavaScript to check if the browser supports SIMD. How do I SIMD?

There are three ways to leverage SIMD: Automatic vectorization: &[i32].sum() Portable SIMD abstractions: i32x4 + i32x4 Platform-specific intrinsics - hang on, we're gonna need a bigger code block: # [ cfg ( all ( any ( target_arch = "x86" , target_arch = "x86_64" ), target_feature = "sse2" ))]

# [ cfg ( all ( target_arch = "aarch64" , target_feature = "neon" ))]

vaddq_u32 ( int32x4_t , int32x4_t ) Let's look at what each one entails and what the state of each programming model is. Automatic vectorization

Just write plain Rust…

Impact beyond crawl scope depends on what the crawler then fetches and is not claimed here. Projects generated from the StormCrawler Maven archetypes are not affected, because all three shipped filter configurations set both parameters. Operators whose configuration sets only `ignoreOutsideDomain` will find the crawl restricted to the source domain, as configured, which may reduce the number of outlinks accepted. items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward generalized coding with our first loop transformer
What VP != VNP Means (In 3 Minutes)
items.summary: math
items.content:
I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted ?

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:

det ( 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ) = 1 ⋅ ( 5 ⋅ 9 - 6 ⋅ 8 ) - 2 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 9 - 6 ⋅ 7 ) + 3 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 8 - 5 ⋅ 7 ) = 0 The naive way is fine for 3 × 3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Θ ( n ! ) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big n × n matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time ( there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method ).

A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. It’s like a determinant without any subtraction:

perm ( 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ) = 1 ⋅ ( 5 ⋅ 9 + 6 ⋅ 8 ) + 2 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 9 + 6 ⋅ 7 ) + 3 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 8 + 5 ⋅ 7 ) = 450 Unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete ), it would be pretty important if there were a way.

What the Anthropic proof that VP ≠ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:

This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn’t clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.

items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Lua for data representation
items.summary: lua
items.content:
my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]] . however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]) . the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===] , not with a ]] or a ]==] , or a ]====] .

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:

return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs)

of course, you can just use string.format with %q , but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

anyway, download this file . if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.

if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.

return (function() arbitrary_code() end)()

trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:

assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))()

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias

consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis

fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero

temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda

programming in lua provides a real world example of this .

the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Cameras Built to Catch Criminals Are Helping ICE Hunt Immigrants
items.content:
Federal immigration agents are using license plate cameras to identify people for deportation, sometimes during random vehicle checks, according to a Nov. 23 investigation by The Atlantic that documented three shootings involving the technology, two of them fatal. The findings raise new concerns in the District, where police operate dozens of license plate readers that can record the movements of residents who are not suspected of crimes.

“We have a lot of concerns about whether or not there’s a constitutional question that needs to be addressed there,” D.C. police union President Gregg Pemberton said in September.

The Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) reported operating 98 fixed license plate readers and 68 mobile readers as of January, including 71 cameras supplied by Flock Safety. The technology photographs passing vehicles, records their locations, and allows investigators to search for particular license plates.

The Atlantic described a Sept. 20 encounter in Austin, Texas, where ICE officers identified a Toyota Corolla registered to Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man facing deportation. Officers attempted to stop him, and he drove away, striking an officer with his side mirror. During a subsequent confrontation, an officer shot him in the back. Garcés Pérez survived and faces a federal assault charge.

At a court hearing, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) investigator Rick Bazan testified that officers had been “doing random checks on vehicles and at random places.”

The Atlantic also connected license plate reader use to fatal ICE shootings in Houston and Maine in July.

Peter Mina, a former senior DHS civil rights official, warned that the technology “creates the potential for rampant civil-rights and civil-liberties abuses.”

“I can’t imagine that all of a sudden someone in the chain of command is going to start monitoring and disciplining people, or counseling them, because they are indiscriminately using license-plate readers,” Mina told The Atlantic. “Because they’re probably feeling the same pressure to produce.”

A July 22 investigation by The Washington Informer documented the nationwide reach of the cameras through DeFlock Maps, a public project identifying more than 117,000 readers and 6,424 law enforcement agencies participating in information-sharing networks.

Only about 900 agencies maintained public transparency portals, while roughly 530 disclosed their data-sharing partners.

“We’ve already seen how this mass surveillance tool can be weaponized and abused by law enforcement,” ACLU officials said.

MPD defended the cameras as “vital proactive investigative tools” for recovering stolen vehicles and weapons and locating missing or wanted people.

ICE is testing a mobile application connected to ELITE, a Palantir-developed system that combines immigration files, addresses, vehicle registrations, criminal records and biometric information. Officers can photograph a plate and retrieve a person’s case file, and the system also generates neighborhood maps identifying concentrations of potential immigration targets.

Department of Homeland Security privacy rules prohibit random plate searches and stops based solely on database results. The Atlantic reported that ICE is developing additional restrictions, but they have not been finalized.

Flock Safety denies providing its technology directly to DHS, and the company says local police departments control access to their records, although privacy advocates have documented immigration-related searches through participating agencies.

Public acceptance of such surveillance depends heavily on its purpose. A September National Policing Institute survey found that 54.4% opposed local license plate reader programs. While 88.3% accepted their use to locate missing children, only 26.4% approved of their use for immigration enforcement. Nearly 58% said stronger safeguards would increase their support.

items.title: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
items.content:
For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange .

Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know.

Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.

Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out.

Microsoft has not announced the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online:

None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud.

For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year.

The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client.

Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies.

Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell ·

It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance . It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Wiki.alpinelinux.org has been languishing a bit

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

items.title: Z, the Bitmap Brothers' Unusual 1996 RTS, Has Been Recreated in 3D
items.content:
Back in 1996, real-time strategy games were enjoying something of a golden age. Command & Conquer had arrived the previous year, Warcraft II was proving enormously popular, and PC players were becoming accustomed to harvesting resources, constructing enormous bases and assembling armies before sending them off to destroy somebody else's carefully arranged buildings. Then the Bitmap Brothers released Z , a real-time strategy game that threw much of that conventional wisdom out the window, in its own way.

Rather than worrying about mining resources or constructing buildings, players controlled an army of argumentative robots fighting over territory. Capture a flag, take control of the surrounding land, and any factories within it became yours. The more territory you controlled, the faster your factories produced reinforcements. It was an unusually aggressive approach to strategy gaming, with battles frequently decided by who could grab an important piece of ground first.

Thirty years later, a group of enthusiasts has revisited that distinctive formula with OpenZ , a free, open-source remake that reconstructs the original game's battlefields and robotic armies in full 3D. The project has been progressing rapidly since its October debut, with version 1.5 having released on 17 November.

GitHub - playopenz/OpenZ: OpenZ: the faithful open-source 3D fan remake of Z (The Bitmap Brothers, 1996) for its 30th anniversary. Free, never sold, 100% original assets.

OpenZ: the faithful open-source 3D fan remake of Z (The Bitmap Brothers, 1996) for its 30th anniversary. Free, never sold, 100% original assets. - playopenz/OpenZ

When strategy games borrowed from the arcade

The Bitmap Brothers had already established an impressive reputation by the time Z arrived. Founded by Mike Montgomery, Eric Matthews and Steve Kelly in 1987, the British studio was responsible for games including Xenon , Speedball 2 , Gods and The Chaos Engine , becoming particularly associated with the Amiga and Atari ST.

Z was something of a departure, although its frantic gameplay retained much of the studio's arcade sensibility. In a 2019 interview with Galaxus , Montgomery explained that development had begun approximately four years before release, initially targeting the Amiga. As the industry changed, the project moved to PC, and the arrival of CD-ROM technology encouraged the team to expand its presentation with animated sequences and a rather distinctive cast of characters.

The result was a game starring two competing robotic armies, red and blue, fighting across deserts, volcanic landscapes, jungles and cities. Their commanders were accompanied by soldiers with names like Grunt, Psycho and Sniper, while the animated sequences followed the exploits of two particularly unprofessional robots, Alan and Brad. It was way more humorous than most competing strategy games, but that didn't make it any easier.

Montgomery recalled that the studio spent months balancing its multiplayer gameplay and deliberately made the computer opponent challenging. The team even adjusted the difficulty for different markets, believing that British players were particularly accustomed to demanding games.

That arcade influence was deliberate. Hesitate too long while capturing territory, and the enemy could quickly gain enough of an advantage to overwhelm you. Losing a single factory or important flag could change the entire battle.

OpenZ is an unofficial fan project created to celebrate the original game's thirtieth anniversary. Its developers have taken the unusual approach of reconstructing the experience with modern technology rather than simply updating the original graphics or running the DOS release through an emulator.

items.title: Stop force-feeding AI to your developers
items.content:
Steve Fenton Nov 23, 2026 8 min read Originally published at thenewstack.io

It’s great that you want your developers to be productive. They want this, too. What I struggle to understand in many managers is the stark contrast between their directive adoption of brute-force AI and their indifference to straightforward techniques that have been proven to be more impactful than coding assistants.

This isn’t a new problem; it’s common for a top-down productivity drive from management to be a smokescreen that hides a deeper problem in their organization. Often, the underlying issue is managers who have lost touch with their teams’ work.

There’s a rather unsavoury practice called “gavage”, which is the process of force-feeding a duck or goose through a tube to increase the size of its liver by up to ten times. The mentality of “force more in, get more out” is how many managers approach AI adoption.

Unsurprisingly, there are animal welfare concerns with this approach, and some countries have banned force-feeding and the production, import, and sale of foie gras . If you’re a developer, there is no law to prevent the force-feeding of AI into your workflow. You depend on having great leaders who want real outcomes.

Like all technology, AI needs an adoption strategy that starts small, tracks its impact, and encourages experimentation at the ground level. You can achieve successful outcomes by engaging developers and allowing them to explore tools, determining where they are most helpful and how to integrate them into daily workflows.

You don’t find many developers who don’t want to be productive. Over the past three decades, most of the complaints I’ve heard from developers are about obstacles that hinder their progress. Their desire to deliver high-quality software drives their efforts to acquire better computers, additional screens, and secure a budget for a cloud test runner.

These have a comparable annual cost to the license for an LLM-based tool. Getting a machine with double the RAM, an extra monitor that you’ll use for several years, or a faster build server are all small costs compared to a developer’s salary. Increased developer productivity pays back at a higher-than-salary rate if you create valuable software.

If you make developers beg for better kit or tools while forcing them to use the AI tools you selected, I question whether you are motivated by productivity. Some other organizational pathology is in play here, and this path leads away from success.

Most developers want to experiment with LLM-based tools. They want to compare different options and see how they fit into the overall picture. You need them to take this experimental approach, as this technology is still in its infancy. Working out where it makes a meaningful difference will take time and knowledge sharing.

If you genuinely want productive developers, start with the productivity blockers they are already raising to you.

Five productivity ideas to try before “More AI”

There have been several studies on the productivity benefits of AI. An expectation was set for some multiplicative factor benefit, like 2x or 10x productivity improvements. While you may achieve these numbers on an example task, they don’t accrue to the organization unless you look at the whole value stream.

The real-world productivity benefit of LLM-based tools is typically between 5% and +20%.

Assuming you’ve given your developers the basic tools of the trade (fast computers, plenty of screen real estate, the best development tools), here are five developer productivity boosts that all beat AI in terms of impact, based on research by DX .

Some people are more productive in the morning, while others hit their peak productivity late in the afternoon. Everyone is different, but they all have something in common: Nobody is productive when their day is stacked full of meetings.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Is Getting Worse at the Exact Moment That Nvidia Rehired Him: It's metastasizing.
items.content:
Much like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman before him, Nvidia’s leader Jensen Huang was summarily pushed out of the company he founded — only to be reinstated after days of turbulence.

Less than an hour before the opening bell, Nvidia announced on Monday morning that it was reinstating its disgraced CEO “effective immediately” after 11 days of mounting losses . The move, an effort personally spearheaded by president Donald Trump , had investors elated, restoring well over 30 percent of Nvidia’s market value.

But while a triumphant Wall Street pops bottles, the underlying scandal is metastasizing. At the core is the Trump administration’s efforts to clear the path for deals Nvidia struck with Chinese companies, seemingly in defiance of export bans and growing concerns over national security amid the AI race.

As the New York Times reported over the weekend , the woman with whom Huang had an extramarital affair with, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from early 2025 until the fall of this year. Even her husband, Kang Wei, had personally worked with the spy agency, according to the newspaper’s sources.

Put simply, Nvidia’s CEO was having an affair with a woman who seems to have been actively relaying information to China’s intelligence community. While we don’t know what kind of data she managed to gather, it’s the best indication yet that Nvidia’s founder is a possibly compromised target of the Chinese government, further highlighting the stakes at play.

Alice Huang was also an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which has been linked to efforts to smuggle Nvidia’s sought after AI chips into China, evading export control laws.

In other words, Trump appears to be directly aiding the Chinese spy agency’s efforts by ensuring Huang’s reinstatement as the linchpin of not just the AI industry, but increasingly the entire US economy .

According to the NYT , the Trump administration was monitoring Alice Huang’s contact with the spy agency for over a year. Experts told the newspaper that China’s Ministry of State Security is explicitly working to get around US export bans.

In the meantime, Trump took to his social media network, Truth Social, this week to trivialize Huang’s extramarital affairs and play them off as a big joke.

That’s despite knowing full well of what was going on. According to the NYT , Trump was briefed on at least two occasions of Alice Huang’s ties to the Chinese spy agency and her affair.

The president has since denied he knew “that she is a spy.”

“Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said in a Friday statement, while calling for Huang’s reinstatement.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to probe the matter, with senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) calling the decision to bring Huang back as CEO “ reckless .”

So far, scheduled intelligence briefings have either been delayed or raised more questions than answers for lawmakers, as the NYT reports.

items.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
items.content:
“It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

Surveillance pricing versus dynamic pricing

Surveillance pricing, according to the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center ( EPIC ), is an algorithmic pricing practice that charges individuals or groups of individuals different prices “for the same goods or services.”

“The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains .

Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart says the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.

Dynamic pricing , or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.

While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.

For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target said that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

ZipRecruiter was one of the first companies to leverage surveillance pricing as we think of it today. In 2018, its profits increased 84 percent by using surveillance pricing versus charging every customer $99. Surveillance pricing is still somewhat nascent, but its potential lucrativeness and the growing availability of user data suggest it may become more common.

Other technological advancements, including advanced machine-learning methods, have further facilitated the growth of personalized pricing.

In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said at least 250 companies used surveillance pricing.

According to a 2025 statement from then-FTC Chair Lina M. Khan, “retailers frequently use people’s personal information to set targeted, tailored prices for goods and services—from a person’s location and demographics, down to their mouse movements on a webpage.”

Surveillance pricing has become more widespread as food delivery platforms, rideshare services, rental housing providers, and other businesses have gained access to the technology and data needed to implement it. Third-party data brokers, advertising and analytics companies, and credit providers make it easy for organizations to get the information needed to build customer profiles. The growth of web browsing, the Internet of Things, and user tracking have created data-rich digital lives that are simple for retailers to analyze.

items.title: Nespresso's project to reduce grams of coffee per capsule
items.content:
Information on Nespresso's Project Olympus.

Date: November 1, 2026 Author: Alvin Bunk

The article is about Nespresso’s internal project to basically reduce the amount of grams per capsule that they produce. In August of 2026, I was informed by a Nespresso internal employee about “Project Olympus”. At first I didn’t think much of it and wasn’t sure how to deal with the information. It seems based on the docs that they were possibly improving the formulas, but I still questioned how that is possible with a reduction of grams of coffee.

The below text is the actual Project Olympus internal text for everyone’s reference to review:

Innovation is at the heart of Nespresso. Our development teams are constantly exploring ways to improve how we roast and grind our coffees-while delivering the same consistent, high-quality results in every cup.

Project Olympus reflects this effort: a behind-the-scenes optimization designed to maintain excellence, even as we evolve our processes.

In some cases, consumers may notice that certain capsules feel lighter than before or ask about possible changes. If inquiries arise, teams should emphasize:
