items.title: UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity
items.summary: compsci, science
items.content:
UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the  School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden said.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”

Dr Andrew Groszek said the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek said.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”

Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.)

Professor Matthew Davis said the UQ team had established an important underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis said.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances .

Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. items.title: Insurers Are Refusing to Cover AI Mistakes in 2026: What It Means for Your Job
items.content:
The biggest names in corporate insurance are quietly pulling AI out of their standard policies, and the timing should put every knowledge worker on alert. AIG, WR Berkley, and Great American have all filed regulatory paperwork in 2026 to exclude AI-related claims from commercial coverage, while Berkshire Hathaway and Chubb have already won approval to do the same. The result is a fast-growing coverage gap that pushes accountability for AI mistakes away from carriers and onto the humans who clicked "approve." If you work alongside AI tools, your AI fluency and documentation habits are now a job-security issue, not just a productivity hack.

The retreat started with math. Generative-AI-related lawsuits in the United States grew nearly 1,000% between 2021 and 2025, and underwriters realized their existing commercial liability and errors and omissions policies were never priced for the new risk surface. The Air Canada chatbot case, where a British Columbia tribunal held the airline liable for a hallucinated bereavement-fare policy, gave carriers a concrete example of what a single bad model output can cost. That ruling, combined with a string of copyright and discrimination claims against companies using generative tools, reinforced how fragile AI rollouts can be when employers cut corners on governance .

WR Berkley filed an absolute AI exclusion for directors and officers, errors and omissions, and fiduciary lines that cuts coverage for "any actual or alleged use, deployment, or development of Artificial Intelligence." AIG told regulators it has no immediate plans to invoke its filing but wants the option as claim frequency rises. Great American is on the same path. According to industry reporting, state regulators have approved more than 80% of these exclusion requests, which means the carve-outs are already live in renewal cycles hitting employer policies this quarter.

The deeper fear is correlated, systemic loss. Kevin Kalinich, who runs cyber at Aon, told reporters the industry can absorb a $400 million or $500 million loss from one company whose agentic AI delivered the wrong price or the wrong diagnosis. What it cannot absorb is an upstream model failure that triggers 1,000 or 10,000 simultaneous losses across every customer running the same vendor. Chubb has signaled it will continue covering some AI incidents but draw a hard line at any event capable of cascading across multiple insureds at once. That is the moment when underwriters stop calling AI "the next cyber" and start calling it uninsurable. The pullback is also rippling into deal economics, because acquirers and lenders use reps-and-warranties insurance to backstop AI exposure, and enterprise rollback rates on AI agents are already running high .

The exposure is not evenly distributed. Tech firms feel it first because their products embed AI directly, and any defective output, biased recommendation, or hallucinated answer flows straight into a customer's workflow. Software engineers, ML researchers, product managers, and customer-experience leads now sit inside a liability chain their predecessors never had to think about. The pattern is sharpest at companies still figuring out which roles AI replaces and which it augments, including the forward-deployed engineer roles that have become the most in-demand tech jobs of 2026 precisely because they sit between the model and the customer.

items.content:
cgo's pointer check is all over the place

cgo does syntactic transformations unaware of Go types, allowing almost unnoticeable changes in source code to turn a 48ns call into a 76µs call. And its correctness checks can panic on legal code, while being exhaustive and expensive in some cases and lax in others.

Shraddha Agrawal Artwork by Andrea Chersia Focus

You are getting early access to this article as a subscriber. Your support makes articles like this possible. Thank you. In this article, we recap some of the basics of Go 's Foreign Function Interface (FFI), cgo , and take a look at example programs that explain its behavior and limits. In particular we'll show how passing the same pointer to C can panic on code that the docs allow, how it can be about 1600x slower depending on how the C call is written, and when the cgo argument checker just gives up. Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started. sudo apt-get install -y clang

curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz

sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz

export PATH = /usr/local/go/bin: $HOME /go/bin: $PATH

go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest

cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well! Consider this program. package main

sum := C . add ( C . int ( 3 ), C . int ( 4 ))

fmt . Println ( "sum (calculated by C code in Go):" , int ( sum ))

main.go Let's walk through each element that cgo introduces: import "C" : This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go. Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C" . This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content: normal C code C include statements C references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add() , C.int We can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build . $ go build main.go

It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper! cmd/cgo: the build-time utility #

go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo , a command line tool. cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary. Let's look at the file generation step in detail. cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code. For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int . In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int . Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory. $ go tool cgo main.go

$ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go

$ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g'

sum : = ( _Cfunc_add )( _Ctype_int ( 3 ) , _Ctype_int ( 4 ))

For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely. items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is really about the death of the American Dream
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is really about the death of the American Dream

Even when they were well written, every GTA story has ultimately been about solving your problems with the accumulation of wealth. But Grand Theft Auto 6 specifically focuses on the systemic issues that make any version of the American Dream — saving money, buying a home and supporting a family with a fulfilling job — incredibly difficult for people living on the margins of society. The crushing weight of capitalism is always pressing down on you, just like in the real world.

Lucia Caminos committed an ill-conceived robbery, is subsequently sent to jail and is forced to claw her way back into civilian life with little support. Jason Duval joined the Army to escape his troubled youth and ends up serving as muscle for a small-time criminal. Much like the real Bonnie and Clyde, Lucia and Jason are driven by the need to escape poverty, but it's up to you to determine if they'll share a similar end.

I only have around 12 hours of GTA 6 under my belt so far (it's estimated to take around 50 hours to beat, and hundreds of hours to fully complete), but Rockstar clearly frames why our lead characters pursue a life of crime: beyond the generational poverty and lack of upward mobility, Lucia and Jason are also trying to build enough stability to reclaim custody of their infant son.

When she decides to stick up a payday loan store (the existence of which is inherently predatory against low-income people ), she's doing it to feed her kid, afford diapers and survive as a single mother. (Jason isn't aware of him at that point in the story.) It's hard to imagine Lucia making such a desperate decision if she had enough social support. But of course, that's not the American way.

Six months worth of baby formula costs upwards of $2,700 in the US,, whereas it's just $759 in the UK. And while America ranks fifth when it comes to the affordability of diapers changes worldwide, that's still around $1,200 a year — a significant cost for poor families. Lucia is lucky that her infant son is placed into kinship care with her aunt, instead of general foster care. Many kinship caregivers receive foster stipends to support their charges , and fostered children also receive Medicaid for free and low-cost healthcare. Ironically, biological parents don't get automatic state support for their kids, and Medicaid eligibility depends on the family's income.

Jason has his own problems. He left the Army after unspecified "trouble" and later worked for a low-grade private security firm. Given his testy relationship to the military, he says he can't receive any veteran home loan benefits , and that may also extend to other assistance, like employment transition and healthcare. He learns that it's easier to use the skills he's gained from the military as a tool for criminal violence, instead of following a more acceptable path like construction. He recommits to Lucia while she's in prison, and GTA 6 begins with him learning that she's about to be released with close supervision. (She's getting out not because of any legal changes in her case, but because her women's prison is too full.)

Jason gets to work rebuilding a small seaside home on loan from his criminal boss (played by the great character actor Stephen Root). It's clear he can put up drywall and nail down roof tiles. But even as he prepares for a more domestic life, he's pulled deeper into the criminal underworld. It gets him some extra cash, but it also makes him a less suitable caregiver for the son he's never met.

After Jason brings Lucia home from jail, it becomes all the more clear how difficult their life is going to be. GTA 6 centers heavily on their relationship (doing things like fixing up the house early on earns Lucia's favor, to the anger of online incels ). This vulnerability may allow an attacker with access to the affected functionality to manipulate database queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized access to or modification of firewall-related data. Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-24T09:34:55.338Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-134894
